title: Pan-American Highway
description: Network of roads in the Americas
wiki_lead:
The Pan-American Highway is a vast network of roads that stretches about 30,000 kilometers (19,000 mi) from Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, United States, in the northernmost part of North America, to Ushuaia, Argentina, at the southern tip of South America. The highway connects 14 countries: Canada, the United States, Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Chile, and Argentina.
No road in the U.S. (except Alaska) or Canada is officially designated as part of the Pan-American Highway, which officially begins at the Mexico–United States border in Nuevo Laredo and runs south.
The Pan-American Highway is interrupted at the Darién Gap, a roadless, dense rainforest area between Panama and Colombia. No road traverses the Gap, and no car ferries have operated in the area for decades; drivers often opt to send their car by cargo ship from one country to the other. North and South America are separated by this 106km (66 mi) gap.

No road traverses the Gap, and no car ferries have operated in the area for decades; drivers often opt to send their car by cargo ship from one country to the other. North and South America are separated by this 106km (66 mi) gap.


Concept of the highway
The highway was built in stages. The first, not long after one could drive across the United States on a paved road, was the highway from Laredo, Texas, to Mexico City. The second stage was the Inter-American Highway to Panama City; previously there were no roads, and little commerce between most Central American countries. There was no road between Costa Rica and Panama until, concerned about access to the Panama Canal in a war situation, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began a highway in 1941.
The third stage, which has not been completed and may never be, continues onward to the southern tip of South America at Tierra del Fuego National Park, near Ushuaia, Argentina. Both Panama and Colombia, as well as environmentalists, are opposed to building a highway through the Darién Gap that separates the two continents.
A Cuban proposal that was not carried out was to include a "circuito del Caribe" (Caribbean circuit). This would have expanded the highway to Puerto Juárez, Mexico (Cancún), and from there by ferry to Pinar del Río, Cuba, from there by road to Havana, and by ferry again to Key West, Florida, and the Overseas Highway. The deterioration of relations between Cuba and the U.S. after the Cuban Revolution of 1959 ended talk of this project.


Development and construction

The concept of an overland route from one tip of the Americas to the other was originally proposed as a railroad. In 1884 the U.S. Congress passed a law with a plan to build an inter-American rail system. This was discussed at the First Pan-American Conference in 1889; however, construction never started. It was abandoned in concept after the independence of Panama in 1903, when work on the canal began.

The system links major existing highways rather than forming a single continuous route, facilitating overland travel, commerce, and cultural exchange while adapting to diverse terrains from Arctic tundra to Andean mountains and Amazonian rainforests. However, it includes no single unbroken path southward, as the highway is interrupted by the DariÃ©n Gap âa roughly 100-kilometer (60-mile) expanse of roadless, swampy jungle and rugged mountains straddling the Colombia-Panama border, rendering vehicular transit impossible without detours by sea or air. Conceived during the 1923 Special Pan-American Conference in Santiago, Chile, as a means to enhance hemispheric connectivity and economic integration, the highway evolved from earlier inter-American infrastructure proposals dating to the late 19th century, with construction accelerating through bilateral U.S. aid and national efforts in the mid-20th century. Key segments, such as the Inter-American Highway in Central America, received targeted funding and engineering support, though progress varied due to logistical challenges, funding shortfalls, and geopolitical hurdles. The network's development symbolized post-World War II aspirations for pan-American unity but faced persistent obstacles, including environmental barriers and debates over bridging the DariÃ©n Gap, where expeditions have repeatedly failed owing to extreme ecological sensitivity, high costs, and risks to indigenous communities and biodiversity. Today, the Pan-American Highway stands as the world's longest drivable road system, enabling epic overland journeys that underscore human engineering triumphs alongside natural limits, though its incomplete status highlights trade-offs between connectivity and preservation in a geopolitically fragmented region.
